title: They Were Just Admitted to the Bar. Now They’re Federal Prosecutors. Meet Trump’s New DOJ.
author: Pratheek Rebala
content:
In early October, a recent law school graduate shared a post on LinkedIn that
would have been unheard of before the second Trump administration.

After passing the bar exam, 29-year-old Preston Bigley wrote, “With this
milestone complete, I will begin serving as an Assistant United States
Attorney in the Criminal Division of the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the
Western District of Texas.”

It was a remarkable achievement, considering Bigley had graduated from Texas
A&M’s law school in May and had been hired by the Justice Department in August
to be, as his resume notes, an “incoming” assistant U.S. attorney. That
unusual title was followed by an unusual caveat: “pending bar admission.” Once
officially licensed to practice the law, he updated his profile to show he had
become a bona fide federal criminal prosecutor.

Bigley is one of a growing cohort of inexperienced attorneys, many of them
fresh out of law school, who are being fast-tracked to fill the shoes of
seasoned career prosecutors who fled or were purged from the DOJ in President
Donald Trump’s second term. That brain drain, amounting to thousands of years
of experience, comes as prosecutions of fraud and drugs have fallen in key
districts to make way for Trump’s immigration agenda, ProPublica found.

Across the country, ProPublica identified more than 50 new assistant U.S.
attorneys with less than three years of experience who traditionally wouldn’t
have been considered for such vital positions, legal experts said. Some were
hired with the intent to anoint them as prosecutors — once they pass the bar
exam, public disclosures show.

That figure is likely a fraction of the actual total, as a comprehensive
analysis is impossible because DOJ staff identities are [redacted in
government personnel data](https://www.opm.gov/policy-data-oversight/data-
analysis-documentation/data-policy-guidance/data-standards/data-release-
policy-december-2024.pdf). But of those ProPublica identified through bar
membership records and social media, about 20 passed the bar within the last
year. At least seven were in the same May graduating class as Bigley, from a
range of schools.

“The fact that the DOJ is hiring, and indeed actively recruiting, right out of
law school — it’s an astounding break with past practice,” said Juliet
Sorensen, a Loyola University Chicago law professor and former assistant U.S.
attorney. “It reflects a lowering of standards for a job that is important and
requires lawyers who are meticulous, committed to doing the right thing, and
bring with them experience beyond just law school.”

To understand how Trump transformed the DOJ, ProPublica examined federal court
data and records, federal workforce and state bar information, and social
media accounts. We also interviewed more than two dozen former assistant U.S.
attorneys.

More than half of those who left the Justice Department in Trump’s first 18
months boasted nine-plus years of legal experience. Those who left had spent,
on average, more than 13 years working for the government, the analysis shows.
Those more experienced attorneys were the ones most likely to take on complex
cases, such as money laundering, organized crime and drug trafficking, legal
experts say and court dockets show.

ProPublica shared its analysis and detailed questions with the DOJ; the
department did not respond. Previously, the DOJ said it “remains committed to
investigating and prosecuting all types of crime.”

### Under Trump’s Second Administration, Newly Hired Assistant U.S. Attorneys
Have Less Experience Than Those Who Departed

![Bar chart comparing assistant U.S. attorney departures and hires by years of
legal experience. Departures far outpaced hires among the most experienced
staff: About 1,100 employees with nine or more years left, while over 400 were
hired. Supervisors saw a similar gap, with about 350 departures and few hires.
Hires outpaced departures for the least experienced groups.
](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/wTitC-.png?w=752)Note:
This analysis of federal pay codes does not include experience ranges for
supervisors. We also exclude some special assistant U.S. attorneys for whom we
cannot infer experience or supervisory status. Pratheek Rebala/ProPublica

The DOJ has long hired recent graduates through its Honors Program, which
places graduates into rigorous training through the main office in Washington,
but experts say the program was small and not meant to replace prosecutors.

Before Trump’s second term, the DOJ typically would not hire new prosecutors
unless they had a minimum of three to five years of legal experience, former
officials and law professors said. That standard is gone. Earlier this year,
[Bloomberg Law reported](https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/doj-to-
allow-hiring-of-us-prosecutors-straight-out-of-law-school), the DOJ waived a
policy requiring at least one year of experience.

While private law firms routinely hire promising graduates before they pass
the bar exam, typically to begin their training, the DOJ’s hiring of new grads
is a striking departure from its once-rigorous hiring process, said University
of Michigan law professor Barbara McQuade, a former U.S. attorney for the
Eastern District of Michigan.

“The people who I hired came to us as partners in law firms,” said McQuade,
who was appointed by President Barack Obama. “These were superstars who had
been very successful at large law firms or in state court prosecutors’
offices.”

Trump’s creation of a less experienced DOJ will have longstanding
consequences, McQuade said.

“It means that some very serious crimes will go unpunished,” she said. “It
takes experienced prosecutors at the federal level to bring down corporate
fraud, transnational gangs and corrupt public officials.”

While experts expressed concern, some of those benefiting from the law school-
to-federal prosecutor pathway have voiced excitement on LinkedIn. “I look
forward to beginning my DOJ career by serving the Del Rio Division,” wrote
Jacquelyn Kilcommons, who graduated from Pace University’s law school in May.
“Upon receiving my bar exam results, I will transition into an Assistant
United States Attorney (AUSA) position.”

As he announced his new role in the district of Washington, D.C., newly
graduated assistant U.S. attorney Ellis O’Donnell wrote, “In the past few
months I have had the honor to graduate from Vanderbilt University Law School
and to sit for and pass the Wisconsin Bar Exam.” ****None of the recent law
school graduates responded to requests for comment.

### Shifting Personnel, Shifting Caseloads

The departure of assistant U.S. attorneys in Trump’s second administration
marks the largest number of exits two years into a presidential term in at
least two decades.

Beyond the personnel turnover, the administration’s priorities have shifted
since Trump retook the White House, an analysis of Federal Judicial Center
data shows.

As immigration cases shot up nationwide, felony fraud prosecutions fell
sharply in key districts. Amid an [exodus of
prosecutors](https://roanoke.com/news/local/crime-
courts/article_9617b556-62de-4c88-8d6f-0e6b06b75b60.html) in the Western
District of Virginia, for instance, fraud cases fell 66%. Those cases dropped
14% in the Southern District of Florida, a hotbed for white-collar crime,
where many prosecutors have left in protest of Trump’s [retribution
campaign](https://www.reuters.com/investigates/special-report/usa-trump-
retribution-tracker/) against people deemed political enemies. Nationally,
drug prosecutions have fallen about 10% in Trump’s first 18 months and fraud
cases are flat.

Meanwhile, the number of people facing immigration-related charges skyrocketed
by almost 50%, clogging the courts and depleting resources at U.S. attorneys’
offices nationwide. Even in border districts where immigration proceedings can
dominate the caseload, prosecutions have risen dramatically. For instance, New
Mexico and the Southern District of California saw 300% and 125% increases in
immigration cases, respectively, the ProPublica analysis shows. In the Western
District of Texas, where Bigley and at least two other recent graduates just
became prosecutors, immigration cases have surged at least 36%.

The immigration caseload, including tens of thousands of unlawful-detention
cases filed in civil court, has strained the department so severely that the
DOJ has drafted hundreds of attorneys from other federal agencies and the
military to keep up, former officials said.

Those cases coincided with violent deportation sweeps led by masked
immigration agents, who [killed U.S.
citizens](https://www.propublica.org/article/alex-pretti-shooting-cbp-agents-
identified-jesus-ochoa-raymundo-gutierrez), and the nationwide protests that
sprouted up in response. Many of the cases Trump’s DOJ brought against people
protesting immigration authorities’ actions fell apart, a [ProPublica analysis
showed](https://www.propublica.org/article/caught-in-crackdown-ice-cbp-doj-
trump-arrests-convictions). The news organization also reported how the
[truthfulness of Trump’s
prosecutors](https://www.propublica.org/article/justice-department-
presumption-of-regularity) has come under question in courts across the
country. The DOJ previously said its attorneys “represent the United States
with integrity.”

Amid the unrest, [ProPublica has tracked nearly ****100,000 habeas corpus
petitions](https://projects.propublica.org/habeas-tracker/) filed by
immigrants arguing that their detentions were unjust. In each case, an
assistant U.S. attorney must defend the government’s position, a task that had
some U.S. attorneys reassigning veteran lawyers — experts in financial crimes,
civil rights and human trafficking — to immigration. In Washington state, an
acting U.S. attorney said he’s so overbooked with unlawful-detention
petitions, his office [cannot handle every
case](https://apnews.com/article/us-attorney-washington-ice-
immigration-9391146bb9f63f1dec4c427dc7716fb2).

![A bearded man in a blue suit and red tie speaks at a podium while flanked by
another man in a blue suit and red tie to his right, and a woman in a blue
business suit and red blouse to his left. Three flags are seen behind the
individuals.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/GettyImages-2276715671.jpg?w=2560)Jason Reding
Quiñones, former U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida, speaks at
the Freedom Tower in Miami in May. Eva Marie Uzcategui/Getty Images

In South Florida, where an exodus of veteran lawyers presaged a drop in fraud
and financial crime cases, one former white-collar crimes prosecutor said he
and his colleagues could not decline an immigration case without permission
from U.S. Attorney Jason Reding Quiñones, who [abruptly
resigned](https://www.miamiherald.com/news/local/article317960596.html) this
month. Before his resignation, Quiñones had led the “grand conspiracy”
investigation targeting former officials Trump alleged were part of a “deep
state” plot against him.

“Every case takes time, and you want to put in effort, and now you’re wasting
your time on cases you don’t believe in or think are unjust,” said the former
prosecutor, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because he hopes to return
to the Justice Department after Trump leaves office. “It affects morale.”

### Ramping Up to Fill the Void

In recent months, the DOJ has ramped up efforts to recruit lawyers to replace
the lost expertise, government data and the department’s recruiting materials
show.

While Justice Department personnel data is kept secret, assistant U.S.
attorneys are [paid on a unique pay
scale](https://www.justice.gov/usao/career-center/salary-information) set by
the attorney general, a quirk that dates to the 1950s and distinguishes them
from other civil servants. By tracking the number of people compensated this
way, it is possible to obtain broad data on the numbers of assistant U.S.
attorneys.

As of January 2025, the department employed about 6,200 assistant U.S.
attorneys, the data shows. Then Trump’s so-called Department of Government
Efficiency took a hatchet to the Justice Department and other federal
agencies. Led by the world’s richest man, Elon Musk, DOGE offered employees
financial packages to resign from the federal government by September 2025.
About 1 in 10 of all assistant U.S. attorney departures were part of that
offer, the data suggests.

The ranks shrank much faster than the department anticipated, former officials
said, and it was unable to hire sufficient replacements. By the end of January
2026, the DOJ lost over 1,300 assistant U.S. attorneys and replaced only about
470 of those attorneys.

### More Assistant U.S. Attorneys Have Departed the Department of Justice
Under Trump Than at Any Time in at Least Two Decades

For most of the past two decades, quarterly AUSA departures held fairly steady
until Trump’s reelection, when they peaked at nearly 500 departures in the
second quarter of 2025.

![Line chart showing Justice Department hires and departures from 2005 through
2026. For most of the past two decades, departures held fairly steady while
hires swung up and down, often outpacing departures. Around the start of the
second Trump administration, departures spiked to by far their highest level
since at least 2005 before falling back toward historical
levels.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/9iFWv-more-
assistant-u.s.-attorneys-have-departed-the-department-of-justice-under-trump-
than-at-any-time-in-at-least-two-decades-.png?w=752)Pratheek Rebala/ProPublica

The DOJ began ****turning to novice attorneys to fill the empty desks.

In early 2026, a former White House official shared a post on X, the social
media platform owned by Musk, that hinted at the DOJ’s growing desperation to
find new hires.

“If you are a lawyer, are interested in being an AUSA, and support President
Trump and anti-crime agenda, DM me,” [wrote Chad
Mizelle](https://x.com/chad_mizelle/status/2017585275896058233), who had
recently left his DOJ role as chief of staff to then-Attorney General Pam
Bondi. Mizelle did not respond to a request for comment.

In March, the department hit its lowest numbers since 2014. A month later, the
University of Miami hosted an event titled [“Lunch & Learn: Entry Level
Opportunities with The U.S. Attorney’s
Office.”](https://events.miami.edu/event/lunch-learn-entry-level-
opportunities-with-the-us-attorneys-office-sdfl) The invite, targeted toward
third-year law students, promised a new pathway to become a criminal
prosecutor in one of the country’s busiest districts.

“The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Florida is now
recruiting 3Ls for entry-level positions beginning immediately after
graduation — an exciting expansion of opportunities for Miami Law students
interested in federal prosecution,” the invitation said.

To lure new hires, the DOJ is [offering signing
bonuses](https://www.justice.gov/legal-careers/job/trial-attorney-252). As of
August, due in part to the hiring spree focused on greener attorneys, the
department lifted its ranks to about 5,600, still a 10% drop from the end of
the Biden administration.

U.S. Rep. Jamie Raskin, the ranking member on the House Judiciary Committee
and the presumed chair once Democrats take charge, told ProPublica that the
shift toward inexperience is showing in courtrooms across the country.

“They’ve sacked some of the finest lawyers in America, by tradition, and
replaced them with a large group of inexperienced lawyers,” said Raskin,
himself an attorney.

In his home state of Maryland, fraud cases fell 31% and drug cases nearly 16%,
while immigration charges nearly doubled. “Those numbers are jaw-dropping,” he
said.

### “Good Time to Be a … Criminal”

Jim Fang was among the veteran prosecutors who left.

Fang’s road to becoming a criminal prosecutor was winding. After working in
tech for about a decade, he switched careers, and in 2009 graduated from
Georgetown Law. He worked in private practice, focusing on intellectual
property law, but couldn’t shake a feeling that what he really wanted was “to
take down bad guys.”

In April 2020, he got his dream job and was named a federal criminal
prosecutor in the District of Nevada. He moved to Las Vegas and, aided by his
11 years handling complex areas of the law, took on tough [white-collar
crime](https://www.justice.gov/usao-nv/pr/us-attorneys-office-
announces-1-funding-hire-prosecutor-combat-unemployment-insurance) cases.

![A man in a gray business suit and silver eyeglasses displays a serious
expression while standing against a tan-colored wall made of thin wood
slats.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/20261112-Whitmore-TrumpsRemadeDOJ-012.jpg?w=527)Jim
Fang, a former federal prosecutor in Nevada, returned to private practice in
2025. Mikayla Whitmore for ProPublica

After the election, Trump picked [Sigal Chattah](https://www.justice.gov/usao-
nv/meet-us-attorney), a former Republican political candidate, to run the
Nevada U.S. Attorney’s Office.

Through court records and sources, ProPublica confirmed that more than 30
staff have left under Chattah’s tenure. The Nevada district is so depleted
that for months [it didn’t have prosecutors in its Reno
office](https://thenevadaindependent.com/article/all-federal-prosecutors-have-
left-dojs-reno-office-as-lawyers-leave-trump-admin-en-masse), about 450 miles
away. Las Vegas prosecutors were asked to fly there for court appearances,
sources said. Chattah disputed the 30 figure but acknowledged that Las Vegas-
based staff flew to Reno “to ensure that our federal and local partners had
competent and aggressive prosecutors.”

The office dropped cases it had been building as Chattah pushed immigration
and [politically motivated prosecutions](https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-
week/trumps-chief-nevada-prosecutor-shirks-doj-orders-boosts-allies). To ease
the caseload, Chattah ordered her civil defense unit, charged with fighting
lawsuits demanding cash from taxpayers, to pay out all cases that could be
settled for $250,000 or less, multiple sources said. “We were ordered to
settle those cases even if they didn’t have merit,” one former assistant U.S.
attorney said. “It was just throwing money at a problem.”

Chattah called the allegations that she issued such a directive “patently
false” and pushed back on her former employees’ characterizations of her
tenure.

“There were attorneys that failed to meet the expectations of competent
workmanship with the Department of Justice, and chose to leave or retire, some
were terminated,” she wrote. “Former AUSAs who failed to handle an expected
case load were replaced with aggressive prosecutors who will keep our state
safe.”

In September 2025, Fang took the DOGE offer and went back into private
practice as a defense attorney. He suspects the department’s loss of financial
crime experts like him will result in fewer successful prosecutions.

“It’s a good time to be a white-collar criminal,” Fang said.

Now facing off against his former colleagues, he’s mostly busy representing
clients who’ve filed habeas petitions. He was recently surprised to learn that
one of the new hires brought into his former office had just passed the bar.
“They’re taking a gamble on them,” he said.

Fang says they may well end up being fine attorneys but added, “There’s no way
I could have taken that job and done it well right out of law school.”

### How We Quantified Changes to Trump’s Justice Department

To measure changes at the Department of Justice under the second Trump
administration, we analyzed federal workforce data from the Office of
Personnel Management and the Federal Judicial Center’s Integrated Database,
which tracks federal court cases.

To measure turnover among assistant U.S. attorneys, we counted the number of
attorneys who were compensated under the [“Administratively Determined” pay
scale](https://www.justice.gov/usao/career-center/salary-information) within
the Executive Office for United States Attorneys and the United States
Attorneys’ Offices (OPM Code: DJ09). To estimate years of legal experience, we
used [experience ranges associated with AD pay
grades](https://www.justice.gov/usao/career-center/salary-
information/administratively-determined-pay-plan-charts). Our workforce
analysis covers January 2025 through August 2026.

To analyze court cases, we looked at the number of defendants charged in
federal court during the roughly 18 months since Trump took office, from Jan.
20, 2025, through June 30, 2026, the most recent data available. We compared
that with a period of the same length (527 days) during the end of the Biden
administration. Each defendant was counted once. We counted only their most
severe charge as ranked by the Federal Judicial Center. We also compared the
last six quarters of Biden’s term with the first six quarters of 2025 and 2026
and found similar results.

We grouped charges into broader categories using a classification system
developed by the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts. Our fraud category
includes embezzlement and forgery. We counted the “Nationality Laws” category,
which the AOUSC groups with fraud, as immigration. We also counted two other
types of charges as immigration offenses: failing to report arrival into the
United States (19 USC 1459) and, in the districts of New Mexico, Western Texas
and Arizona, entering military-designated national defense areas along the
border (50 USC 797).
